confidence_note: Bloom's call for 'rational compassion' and his admiration for effective altruism (citing Peter Singer) are confirmed by reviews and Wikipedia; the Baby Jessica example (Midland, Texas, 1987: a little girl stuck in a well) is confirmed as used by Bloom to show people care more about one visible child than about crises affecting many more. The old TR text's blindness-surgery versus other-disease example, 'dollar per person' figures and 'cold and inhuman' framing could not be verified in the book and are removed. Facts are thin; no figures, no amounts raised, no ages. The book gives no named cost-effectiveness case that could be verified.
facts: Bloom argues that empathy is a poor guide for decisions, though it can motivate kindness.
He contrasts empathy with what he calls rational compassion: caring about others' suffering while using cost and benefit reasoning to decide what to do.

He cites the Baby Jessica case of 1987, in Midland, Texas, where a little girl was stuck in a well, as an example of people caring more about one visible child than about crises affecting many more people.
He holds up the effective altruism movement, inspired by philosopher Peter Singer, as an ideal: directing giving toward where it helps the most people.
Bloom says people can make decisions on considerations of costs and benefits.
scene_details: a little girl stuck in a well in Midland, Texas, in 1987
effective altruism: asking where giving helps the most
tension: One child stuck in a well draws everyone's attention while larger crises affecting many more people get less of it.
opening_idea: In 1987 a little girl was stuck in a well in Midland, Texas, and the world watched; Bloom asks about the larger problems that nobody watched.

lessons.idea: Good intentions are not enough; asking which action helps most can point somewhere different from where your feelings point.
lessons.anchor: The Baby Jessica case versus the effective altruism question of where giving helps most people.

reflect_final: The last time you wanted to help someone, did you check whether your help would actually change their situation, and how would you find out?

use_cases.situation: A team wants to adopt a charity because a colleague told a moving story.
use_cases.move: Ask what the charity achieves per unit of money and compare it with one or two alternatives before voting.

use_cases.situation: A relative asks for a loan after an emotional appeal.
use_cases.move: Say you want to help and ask what would change their situation most, rather than giving the quick yes.

use_cases.situation: You are about to donate after seeing one photo online.
use_cases.move: Bloom points to the Midland well rescue as a case of attention going to one child; look up one comparison charity first.

pocket_idea: A child in a well gets the world's attention; rational compassion asks where the same help does the most good.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A girl in a well in 1987 got the world's attention, while larger crises affecting many more people got less.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Paul Bloom points to a 1987 case in Midland, Texas, where a little girl was stuck in a well and everyone cared, while crises affecting many more people drew less attention. He doesn't ask us to stop caring. He asks for rational compassion: use feeling to start, then ask where help does the most good, as effective altruists do.
